📖 Plain-English guide — what every label on this dashboard means (tap to open)
The engines & tabs
TCE (Trend Convergence Engine) — the core stock-picker. It checks 9 separate signals on a stock and rates it HIGH / WATCH / IGNORE by how many line up (“converge”) at once.
Conviction — how many of the 5 strongest signals (the ones about the business actually improving) are firing. A US stock reaches HIGH only if at least 4 fire.
GUARD (relative-strength guardrail) — did the stock beat the overall US market (the SPY S&P-500 fund) over the last 6 months, and by how many points. If it’s losing to the market it “vetoes” a HIGH down to WATCH — a stock that can’t keep up with the market doesn’t earn top conviction. (“+183pt” = beat the market by 183 percentage points.)
EXPLOSIVE screen — a separate filter that flags young companies with fast, accelerating growth: tomorrow’s potential big winners, caught early.
Multibagger tabs — curated watchlists of names that could multiply in value; the engine’s job here is to confirm strength, not whether the stock is cheap today.
IM3 — the fundamental quality score, out of 162 points, graded A/B/C/FAIL. It answers “is this a financially sound business,” separately from price.
IG2 / Banking InvestoGenie 2.0 (“System B”) — banks can’t be judged like factories, so banks use this dedicated 24-ratio / 48-point bank model instead of IM3.
The chips on each row
V · G · M (Style) — Value (is it cheap?), Growth (growing & speeding up?), Momentum (is the market already moving on it?). Describes a stock’s style; never changes its rating. A Low Value (expensive-looking) is normal for an early winner — context, not a penalty.
Trend (vs 200-DMA) — ▲ Uptrend = price above its 200-day average (healthy); ▼ Downtrend = below it (falling-knife risk); golden / death = the 50-day average crossing above / below the 200-day (bullish / bearish shift). DMA = day moving average.
The 9 TCE signals: News = press coverage · Insider = company insiders buying their own stock (SEC filings) · Vol = today’s volume vs a normal day · Mom = recent price momentum · Margin = profit growing faster than sales (getting more profitable) · Capital = short interest (how many bet against it) · EPS-rev / Rev-rev = analysts raising or cutting forecasts · Target = upside to the average analyst price target · Rec = share of analysts saying “buy.”
▲FWD = analysts expect next year’s earnings to jump and/or just raised estimates · ⚡Z #1/#2 = the stock’s Zacks Rank (#1 Strong Buy, #2 Buy — the estimate-revision model).
Scores & valuation
IM3 grades: A ≥80% · B ≥60% · C ≥50% · FAIL <50% (banks: ELITE ≥85% · STRONG ≥75% · SOLID ≥60% · FAIR ≥50% · WEAK). IV = estimated fair price · MoS = margin of safety (how far below fair value the price is; positive = cheap) · PEG = P/E ÷ growth (under ~1 = growth is cheaply priced) · CAGR = compound annual growth rate · CFO = cash from operations · ROE = return on equity.

Green verdict vs MoS — two lenses, by design: the green EXPLOSIVE call comes from the growth engine (accelerating revenue/profit, cash-backed); the IV / MoS / Valuation chips are the value lens, shown for context only — a rich price never vetoes an explosive call, because tomorrow's big winners usually look expensive on trailing numbers early (your own multibagger rule). Red MoS beside a green verdict is the two lenses honestly disagreeing — honest disagreement, not an error.
Markets & macro
PSX = Pakistan Stock Exchange · KSE-100 = its main index · SPY = the S&P 500 (US market benchmark) · SBP = State Bank of Pakistan (sets the policy rate) · Rupee value vs trading partners = the rupee measured against the currencies Pakistan actually trades with, after inflation (is the rupee over/under-valued) · CPI / PCE = inflation gauges · DXY = US-dollar index · COT = futures positioning (who’s long/short) · GVZ = gold’s “fear gauge” · WALCL = the size of the US Fed’s balance sheet.
Tab 16 — World ETF Engine
UCITS = a European-regulated fund structure. As a UAE resident, buying Irish or Luxembourg-domiciled UCITS ETFs (rather than US-domiciled ones) avoids US estate-tax exposure above $60,000. Every fund on this tab is a UCITS ETF, buyable on IBKR.
The four doors — four independent ways the engine can recommend a fund: Country door (a country’s stock market beat the dollar over 6 months, ranked in the top 3) · Sector door (a US sector is scored Booming or Favoured) · Theme door (one of 4 global groupings — Asia-Tech, Developed-West, Commodity-Bloc, Emerging — is Booming or Favoured; Asia-Tech also triggers a dedicated semiconductor pick) · EM ex-China door (emerging markets overall are strong but China specifically is not, so a fund holding EM stocks minus China is recommended instead of a broad EM fund).
Double-confirmed (★) — the SAME fund was independently recommended by two different doors at once. This is not a stronger opinion from one signal — it is two separate calculations agreeing. Shown in plain text on each card (e.g. “ranked #1 country by return AND is the top country driving a Booming theme”).
Momentum-Watch — a separate list of the 55 non-leveraged UCITS funds already up 35% or more this year, plus the top 5 Nasdaq-100 trackers added on request despite sitting below that bar (real US mega-cap tech coverage, clearly marked as the exception they are). This is not the engine’s advice — it is an observation list of what is already running, so strong performers outside the engine’s own doors don’t go unseen.
Hydrogen Watch — 4 hydrogen-economy funds tracked separately because they were missing ISINs (fund ID codes) in the main data file and had to be sourced individually; shown as a distinct thematic list, not an engine recommendation.
Metals ETC Watch — gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and copper ETCs (Exchange-Traded Commodities — the metal itself, held in a vault, not a company; copper is the one synthetic/futures-based exception). Paired with the live trend, RSI, and (gold/silver/copper) COT positioning already shown on Tab 12 Metals.

FY2026-27 Federal Budget — Fiscal Stance & Sector Tax Map

What this is: a plain-language read of the federal budget (presented 12–13 Jun 2026) and which sectors its taxes help or hurt. It is a top-down sector read only — it never changes any individual stock’s grade, valuation or whether it is screened.

Fiscal stance (consolidation under the IMF programme): outlay Rs18.77tn (+7%) · GDP-growth target 4% · inflation target 8.2% · Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) revenue Rs15.26tn · fiscal deficit 3.6% of GDP · primary surplus 2% · interest Rs8.05tn (+16%) · defence Rs3tn (+15.6%). Debt servicing alone is over half the budget — relief on one side is paid for by base-broadening on the other. State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) policy rate held at 11.5%, so the ≥11% defensive trigger stays ON.

🟢 Budget-favoured (tailwind)🔴 Budget-pressured (headwind)
Cement / Real estate / Steel — property withholding tax cut (2.5→1.25% buy, 5.5→2.75% sell), Rs1tn Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP), Apna Ghar housing.Banks + Fertilizer + E&P — the 2% Super-Tax cut for income >Rs500mn applies to everyone except these three (relative headwind; touches OGDC/PPL/FFC/MCB).
Exporters / Textiles — export advance/min tax cut 2.0→1.25%, export-development surcharge abolished.High-cc autos — SUVs 2,000–3,000cc brought under Federal Excise Duty (FED).
Tech / IT — income-tax exemption extended to June 2029, export-proceeds collection lowered.Refiners / chemicals — new Rs80/litre FED on solvents, naphtha, turpentine.
Consumer / Autos / FMCG — salaried slab cuts, surcharge abolished above Rs12mn, +10% minimum wage. Airlines — intl business-class FED removed.Distributors / wholesalers — minimum tax raised 0.25→0.5%.

Net read: the budget rotates the tax burden toward documented consumption/construction/exporters and leaves the index-heavy old guard (banks, fertilizer, E&P) without the relief others got. Guardrail: this tags the sector wind only — a pressured-sector stock with strong fundamentals still scores Grade A. Direction of tax impact, not buy/sell advice; the budget is at Finance-Bill stage so specific rates can still shift.

Top-Down Engine (M1)

What this tab does: it finds stocks the top-down way — from the big economic picture down to specific names — in four steps: (1) read where the economy is right now, (2) pick the sectors that phase usually favors, (3) list the strongest stocks inside those sectors, (4) squeeze that to a final short list of buys. What you get: the strongest stocks in the sectors today’s economy favors. It only reads live data — it never changes any stock’s grade, valuation, conviction tier or whether it’s screened. How this differs from the US Dashboard: the US Dashboard watches the economy (rates, inflation, recession risk) and never picks stocks; this tab uses that economic read as Step 1 and ends in stock names.

Sector & Stock Implications

US Sectors

Under each sector is a plain vs-market summary — how pricey it is, how profitable, and which way it’s heading — measured against the average across all US sectors, shown as a one-line read plus three quick tags. P/E (price-to-earnings) is how many dollars you pay for each $1 of a company’s yearly profit, so a higher number means investors expect faster growth (or the stock is dearer) and a lower number means modest expectations (or a possible bargain) — a quick gauge of how pricey a sector is for what it earns. Each summary also shows a small quarter trend line (the sector’s price path over the last three months) and, where analyst coverage exists, a forward read of the total return (analysts’ price-target gain plus dividend yield) expected over the next quarter and six months.

⚡ Bottoms Up M2 — the 30% engine

Sector-blind by design. While M1 (Tab 6) picks sectors top-down for the disciplined 70%, this engine scans every company in the universe — favoured sector or not — for early, converging evidence that something big is starting: the price turning, the business inflecting, analysts raising their profit estimates, trading volume surging. It flags, it never filters — every name is an invitation to investigate, not a recommendation.

New — what company insiders are doing with their own money (SEC filings): a \u25b2 insider buying chip means officers or directors bought shares on the open market (SEC Form 4) — the strongest outside confirmation a turnaround is real, and it counts toward a name being flagged. A red \u26a0 chip means the company just filed a material 8-K (bankruptcy, a CFO/CEO leaving, an auditor change, a big write-down) — a warning shown beside the name, never counted as a positive. US-listed names only; Pakistani names show nothing here because they don\u2019t file with the SEC.

Explosive Stocks (US + PSX) — Live Scanner Feed

📊 How to read the Signals (A · B) — what makes a stock EXPLOSIVE

Every stock is judged on two signals. The two dots in the Signals column show whether each one is found (● green = found) or missing (○ hollow = missing).

Signal A — Growth. The business is genuinely growing. It fires only when both are true on the latest annual financials: revenue up more than 20% year-over-year (chip G1) and operating profit up at least 15% (chip G2).

Signal B — Acceleration. Profit is speeding up, not just growing. It fires when operating-profit growth is over 20% and net profit is growing faster than operating profit — the net-profit ÷ operating-profit growth ratio is above 1.0 (chip A1), meaning gains compound as they flow to the bottom line. Guard: if last year’s operating profit was zero or negative, Signal B is held off (you can’t measure acceleration off a non-positive base).

Signal Q — Quarterly early warning. The same test as Signal A, but on one quarter: the most recent quarter versus the same quarter one year ago (never versus last quarter — that would just measure the season). It fires when quarterly sales are up more than 20% and quarterly profit up at least 15%. Because it reads a single fresh quarter, it can flag a company turning up to a year before the annual Signal A can. Important — Q compares only ONE quarter. It is a single-quarter snapshot, not proof the company has grown every quarter in a row: a stock can fire Q on one strong quarter. For a sustained, multi-quarter turnaround, look at Signal T below, which watches several rolling quarters bend upward. Honest note: at the screen level the profit figure is earnings-per-share (a close stand-in for operating profit, which isn't published quarterly for every name).

Signal T — The turnaround hook (T \u21A9). This is the early-turnaround detector. It adds up each company's profit over the last four quarters — a rolling full-year total — and watches that total move quarter by quarter. Because every window holds all four seasons, the seasons cancel out. It lights up when that rolling total either rises two or more quarters in a row after a slump, or crosses from a loss into a profit — the classic shape of a business bending upward, typically 2 to 4 quarters before the annual numbers show it. It's the flagship signal of the Turnaround watchlist (Tab: M2), and appears here as a purple T \u21A9 badge when it fires.

\u2605 Highlighted rows — read the colours. A gold\u2192green row (\u2605 ALL SIGNALS) is the top of the funnel: EXPLOSIVE with all three signals (A, B, Q) firing and a strong quality grade (A/B). If it also shows a live turnaround, it gets the richer gold\u2192green\u2192violet band (\u2605 ALL + T). A plain violet-tinted row (\u21A9 TURNAROUND) is an M2 turnaround name (Signal T fired) — all turnarounds share that tint so they read as one group. These are the names where the signals agree.

How they combine into the verdict:
● + ● both → 🚀 EXPLOSIVE — growing and accelerating
● A only → 📈 QUALITY-GROWTH — growing, profit not yet accelerating
● B only → ⤴ INFLECTION — accelerating off a sub-20% top line (verify the turn)
○ + ○ neither → ✗ NOT EXPLOSIVE — or “OP declining” if operating profit is shrinking

The two dots map onto the detailed Conditions chips beside them: G1 + G2 = Signal A, A1 = Signal B. The other chips (A2 = pre-tax/operating ratio; C1/C3 = cash backing earnings) are extra context, not part of the two core signals. All figures are year-over-year from annual financial statements.

Four Metals — Bias Score & Overlay

Where Institutional Money Is Positioned

Every week, large speculators (hedge funds, managed-money traders — not central banks or physical users) report their futures positions to US regulators. A heavy, one-sided position is a crowd — crowds eventually unwind, which is itself a signal. Real data for Gold, Silver, and Copper; Platinum and Palladium aren't tracked by this feed (COMEX doesn't publish the same weekly report for them at meaningful volume).

What Moves Gold & Silver — World Driver Map
COT Positioning Crowding Gauge
📊 CFTC CMX Non-Commercial Net Positions —
What this shows: how one-sided the big futures bets are. Each bar is the share of bets that are “long” (betting the price rises). Above ~20% means the crowd is heavily piled on one side, which tends to snap back — so read it as a crowding warning, not a buy/sell signal. Timing: the report is taken each Tuesday and published the following Friday, so the latest one always lags a few days (the date shown is correct, not stale).
COT Positioning Index — Stretch & Flip (9 Futures Contracts)
🧭 How stretched is positioning, and which way is it turning —
What this shows: the COT Index turns each contract’s speculator net position into a 0–100 score versus its own last year (1Y) and three years (3Y). Low (≤20) = crowded short / washed-out (often room to rally); high (≥80) = crowded long / extended (often room to fall); the middle is neutral. Flip is the net position as a % of open interest, and the 4w / 13w tags read BUY when the latest flip is above its recent average (positioning improving) or SELL when below. RSI is a momentum read on the net-position line (our own standard RSI, not a cloned proprietary one). Read this as positioning context, not a buy/sell signal on its own.

Pakistan factors (Oil, Interest rates, Currency valuation, Current account, Fiscal account, Inflation, CB Reserves) score the local PKR gold price. Global factors (USD Policy Stance, QE/QT, Recession Fear, Pakistan rupee value, Dollar Index, IMF, Pakistan Default, GeoPolitical Situation) score the international USD gold price. Each factor = +1 Positive / 0 Neutral / −1 Negative. Score range −15 to +15. Scoring bands: ≥5 = STRONG BUY, 2–4 = BUY, 0–1 = NEUTRAL, −1 to −3 = REDUCE, <−3 = AVOID. Seasonality from Bloomberg 2004–2014 averages (Sarmaaya PDFs). Metal propagation via correlation matrix (Sarmaaya Other Metals PDF slide 19): Silver × 0.7, Platinum × 0.5, Palladium × 0.7. COT data: CFTC CMX weekly (non-commercial net positions). GDX top holdings from Sarmaaya PDF slide 19 (Week 11).

World ETF Engine — Global Macro Opportunities (UCITS)

How the engine works (5-stage funnel): Country LEIs signal expansion → select booming countries + US sectors → select the relevant UCITS ETF → check past returns as confirmation → track in results. As a UAE resident you buy these on IBKR as Irish/Luxembourg UCITS funds, avoiding the US estate-tax exposure that comes with US-domiciled ETFs above $60k.

Four doors: Country (top 3 by 6M USD return, Overweight/Hedge signal) · US Sector (top 2 booming sectors) · Global Theme (top 2 themes × top 2 countries — Korea and Taiwan both fire when Asia-Tech is booming, plus a dedicated semiconductor pick) · EM ex-China (fires when Emerging is Booming/Favoured but China itself is Neutral/Avoid). Same ISIN from multiple doors = double-confirmed badge, explained in plain text on the card.

How the ETF matching works — in plain language

What these blocks are. For every stock the dashboard’s own engines pick (M1 top-down and M2 turnaround/quality), we find the closest fund you can actually buy — a UCITS ETF, the tax-efficient type for a UAE resident. You’re never being told to buy the single stock; you’re shown a fund that gives you similar exposure in a better wrapper.

How a stock is matched to a fund (checked in this order, best first): 1· Holding match — the stock is a top holding inside a specific fund (you get real exposure to the name). 2· Specialist match — it belongs to a recognisable theme (chips, clean energy, AI, cybersecurity, space) and gets that specialist fund. 3· Sector match — it maps to its broad sector fund (healthcare, industrials, finance…). 4· Broad fallback — only if nothing else fits does it land in a whole-market fund. The “Match” column on every row tells you which rung it landed on — that’s how you judge the fit: a tight match is a good proxy, a “broad” match means look closer.

Turnaround vs Quality. The M2 screen has two lanes and both are covered here: turnaround (early, speculative inflections) and quality (stronger financials, cleaner setups). Every flagged name in both lanes now gets a fund — earlier only the top-ranked turnaround names did, which is why some names (e.g. CRDO, GEV) were missing before; that’s now fixed.

Why you don’t see one row per stock. Funds are grouped — if 10 healthcare stocks all map to the same healthcare fund, you see one fund row with 10 name-chips, not 10 rows. So a long list of stocks collapses into a handful of ETF rows.

Pakistan names all map to the single Pakistan fund that exists (Chimera, ADX-listed) — it’s thin and illiquid, so it’s a broad wrapper for the whole basket, not a per-stock match. Use limit orders.

About the return numbers. YTD / 1-year / today are US-dollar based, priced live from TradingView. They will not match local-currency sources like investing.com — a fund’s dollar return and its home-currency return differ by the exchange-rate move. The Pakistan fund in particular trades thinly in dirhams, so treat its figure as indicative and verify on the fund factsheet.

M1 / M2 Booming-Sector Themes — where the buy lists cluster

Derived from the engines’ own buy lists: any GICS sector holding ≥2 engine names (M1 + M2 combined) becomes a theme, carrying 3–4 UCITS sector ETFs. Member tickers are colour-tagged by engine (M1 / M2).
How this differs from the other theme lists on this tab: the Engine Recommendations (top of tab) are a macro top-down funnel — country LEIs & global themes pick region/country ETFs. The Emerging Themes Watch (below) is a fixed, curated list of narrow forward-looking themes (AI, cyber, quantum, space…) that have no engine signal — a hand-maintained watchlist. These M1/M2 themes are neither: they’re bottom-up, broad GICS-sector baskets computed live from where your actual stock picks land — so when the buy lists churn, these themes churn automatically (churn = signal). Same sector can appear in more than one list (e.g. IT here vs. narrow AI/semis in Emerging Themes); that’s expected — different lens, different granularity.

Physical Metals ETC Watch

Physical-backed ETCs (Exchange-Traded Commodities) — the metal itself, held in allocated vaults, no equity counterparty risk (Copper is the one exception — it’s a synthetic/swap-based ETC, since copper has no practical physical-vault structure at retail scale the way precious metals do). All 5 metals Tab 12 Metals tracks (Gold, Silver, Platinum, Palladium, Copper) are covered here, each fund grouped under its metal with that metal’s live 200-DMA trend, RSI, and (Gold/Silver/Copper) COT positioning shown directly below the heading — the same numbers Tab 12 computes, wired here so you don’t have to cross-reference tabs to see whether now is a good entry.
